title: Abbreviated lésion score (AIS) pour Inhalation lésion
formula:
Selection of the appropriate findings:

| Features | Grade | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No carbonaceous deposits, erythema, edema, bronchorrhea, or obstruction | 0 | No injury |
| Minor or patchy areas of erythema, carbonaceous deposits, bronchorrhea, or bronchial obstruction present | 1 | Mild injury |
| Moderate erythema, carbonaceous deposits, bronchorrhea, or bronchial obstruction present | 2 | Moderate injury |
| Severe inflammation with friability, copious carbonaceous deposits, bronchorrhea, or obstruction present | 3 | Severe injury |
| Mucosal sloughing, necrosis, or endoluminal obstruction present | 4 | Massive injury |

how_to_use.why:
- No universal consensus exists on grading for inhalation injury. The AIS has been widely utilized as the predominant bronchoscopic inhalation injury severity score in the literature (but have not been compared head to head with other bronchoscopic criteria).
- Of note, a[multicenter prospective cohort study](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/record/NCT01194024)by the American Burn Association is currently underway to develop and validate a scoring system for inhalation injury based on clinical, radiographic, bronchoscopic, and biochemical parameters.
how_to_use.when: Patients adultes chez qui une lésion d'inhalation est suspectée et qui bénéficient d'une bronchoscopie souple.
how_to_use.pearls:
- May predict development of ARDS, length of time on mechanical ventilation, and prolonged ICU stay.
- Some studies have found a non-statistically significant trend towards worse outcomes with higher AIS.
- AIS severity has *not* been consistently associated with mortality ([Sheridan 2016](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27518664)).
- Cannot reliably predict need for high fluid resuscitation requirements.
- A typical flexible bronchoscope is on average 5 mm in diameter. Hence, bronchoscopy can only identify proximal airway changes and not the narrower distal and peripheral airway changes. Thus, bronchoscopic findings cannot be fully relied upon to accurately reflect the overall severity of airway inhalation injury.

next_steps.advice: Une sévérité AIS élevée ne doit pas à elle seule dicter les décisions de prise en charge, qui doivent, comme toujours, être prises conjointement avec l’anamnèse, l’examen clinique et les résultats de laboratoire.
next_steps.critical_actions: Les manifestations macroscopiques d'anomalies des voies aériennes peuvent être retardées et, de ce fait, faussement rassurer le clinicien quant à l'absence de lésion d'inhalation ([Hunt 1975](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1152086)).
next_steps.management:
- Le traitement symptomatique constitue le principal moyen de prise en charge de la lésion d'inhalation, car les options de traitement pharmacologique sont très limitées une fois la lésion d'inhalation constituée.
- La bronchoscopie peut jouer un rôle thérapeutique dans la clairance des voies aériennes, car les tissus nécrotiques et les escarres peuvent former des pseudomembranes, une desquamation de la muqueuse et une obstruction bronchique.
- Les autres mesures comprennent une hygiène bronchique intensive, incluant des bronchodilatateurs (p. ex. agonistes β2 inhalés), une kinésithérapie respiratoire fréquente et une mobilisation précoce du patient.
- L'œdème des voies aériennes supérieures peut s'aggraver, en particulier au cours des premières 24 heures suivant la lésion, rendant l'intubation nécessaire. Si une ventilation mécanique est requise, un mode de ventilation percussive à haute fréquence peut être envisagé, car certaines études ont montré un bénéfice dans cette population de patients. Une stratégie de ventilation protectrice pulmonaire à faible volume courant (6-8 cc/kg de poids corporel prédit) est préférée chez l'adulte.
- D'autres mesures de soutien ont été utilisées avec un succès variable, notamment le décubitus ventral, l'oxygénation par membrane extracorporelle (ECMO), les anticoagulants inhalés (p. ex. héparine, antithrombine) et la N-acétylcystéine (NAC) inhalée.
- De plus, une orientation vers un [centre de grands brûlés désigné](https://ameriburn.org/public-resources/burn-center-regional-map/) doit être envisagée en présence de toute lésion d'inhalation, conformément aux [recommandations de l'American Burn Association](https://ameriburn.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/burncenterreferralcriteria.pdf).

evidence:
The AIS for inhalation injury was first proposed by Endorf and Gamelli in 2007. The purpose of their study was to identify whether severity of inhalation injury correlated better with pulmonary parameters (e.g. lung compliance, PaO~2~:FiO~2~ratio) and acute fluid resuscitation requirements than bronchoscopically assessed inhalation injury severity. They retrospectively reviewed 80 adult patients requiring intubation, mechanical ventilation, and flexible bronchoscopy for suspected inhalation injury within the first 24 hours of admission. They used the AIS classification to separate their patients into two groups of bronchoscopic inhalation injury: one including grades 0 and 1 and another including grades 2, 3, and 4. They compared characteristics, such as fluid resuscitation requirements, initial oxygenation, lung compliance, and duration of mechanical ventilation; only bronchoscopic severity correlated with decreased survival ( *p* = 0.03).

[Hassan et al](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20006445)also found a significant ( *p* <0.01) increase in mortality with bronchoscopic severity. They did not use the AIS.

Since 2007, a number of studies have used AIS in order to establish a clear relationship between bronchoscopic grade of injury and a range of clinical outcomes; however, the results have been varied. For instance, in contrast to Endorf and Gamelli’s study, Albright et al ([2012](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3290689)), Mosier et al ([2012](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21941194)), and Spano et al ([2016](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26594859)) all found that increasing AIS grade did not have a significant effect on mortality, with *p* -values of 0.21, 0.10, and 0.15, respectively.

Albright et al did show that increasing severity was associated with longer ventilator days ( *p* = 0.036) and intensive care unit (ICU) stay ( *p* = 0.040). Additionally, Mosier et al noted a significant association between AIS grade severity and development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) at 24 hours ( *p* <0.01).
